titel: The idea of the index fund
kurz: Why an index fund that only aims to achieve the market average does better than the majority of paid fund managers.

bloecke.md:
An [[Index fund|index fund]] promises less than any other investment product. It does not try to beat the market and only aims to achieve the market's return minus its own costs. That seems unambitious, yet the majority of paid fund managers do not achieve this result over the long term.

The reason can be shown without an empirical study. It follows from a calculation that you can work through in an afternoon and that holds even if you reject the assumption of efficient markets.

## William Sharpe's arithmetic

In 1991, William Sharpe published a short essay in the *Financial Analysts Journal* entitled “The Arithmetic of Active Management”. It begins with two definitions. An investor is passive if they hold all the securities of a market in market weights and change nothing; every other investor is active.

From these definitions follows an identity, that is, an equation that always holds. All investors together hold the entire market, because every share belongs to someone. If you subtract the passive segment, which holds the market exactly in market weights, the active segment is left. Consequently, the active segment as a whole also holds the market in market weights. Before costs, the average actively managed euro therefore earns exactly the market return, by definition and not just approximately. After costs, it necessarily earns less.

Since this result is not based on observations, no new study can refute it either. It depends only on addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. The statement can only be challenged by defining the market differently from the benchmark or by disputing that all holdings together make up the market.

bloecke.formel: Avg. net return (active) = Market return − Avg. costs (active)
bloecke.erklaerung: The first term, the market return, follows from an identity and is not an estimate. How much remains therefore depends solely on costs. What is meant is the capital-weighted average of all active euros, not the average of all funds.
variablen: return on all securities in the market, weighted by market capitalisation
management fee, transaction costs, spreads and tax effects of the active segment
bloecke.beispiel: According to ESMA, equity UCITS in the EU cost 1.50% p.a. over a ten-year horizon when actively managed, and 0.31% as ETFs. The expected gap in net returns is therefore around 1.2 percentage points a year. ESMA measured a gap of 1.0 points compared with ETFs. Compared with index funds that are not exchange-traded, whose costs were 0.97 points lower, the gap was 1.2 points.

bloecke.titel: Costs and net return of equity UCITS in the EU over ten years
bloecke.unter: At 1.2 points (index funds) and 1.0 points (ETFs), the return gaps to the active funds are of the same order of magnitude as the cost gaps of 0.97 and 1.19 points, as the arithmetic would lead you to expect. ESMA, reporting period 2012-2021, geometric mean.

bloecke.md:
## The market average as the yardstick

The word “average” suggests the middle of the field. After costs, however, the market average is mathematically above the average of active investors. A fund manager whose fund costs 1.50% a year has to beat the market by 1.3 percentage points before costs just to draw level with an ETF costing 0.20%. This lead has to be achieved on average year after year. On the other side of the manager's purchases and sales is another active investor doing the same calculation. Before costs, this is a zero-sum game; after costs, it is a loss-making business for active investors as a group.

The measured data fit this. Of the euro-denominated active global equity funds, 98.2% underperformed their benchmark over ten years (SPIVA Europe, as of 30 June 2025). The full figures on time periods, regions and the persistence of winners follow in the lesson on the evidence in module 12. For this lesson, the direction is enough.

A complete picture also includes the counter-criticism. In 2026, Cremers, Fulkerson and Riley showed that the rates are considerably lower if you calculate on a capital-weighted basis, assess funds that were wound up on their performance until they were wound up and compare with actual index funds instead of indices. For US equities, the underperformance rate over 20 years is then around 55% instead of over 90%. The study was funded by the association of active managers, but its results can be checked by recalculating them. Even on this reading, a dollar invested in active funds is about as likely to do better than in an equivalent index fund as to do worse. Costs have already been deducted in this comparison. So even according to this study, no advantage for active funds can be expected on average.

John Bogle's [[Cost matters hypothesis|cost matters hypothesis]] needs no assumption at all about the efficiency of markets. Whether prices process information correctly plays no role in the equation. Gross return minus costs equals net return in every market state. The return is uncertain, whereas the costs are fixed. They are the only part of the equation that an investor knows in advance and determines themselves.

bloecke.titel: Illustrative calculation for €10,000 at a 7% gross return over 30 years
bloecke.unter: Because each year's costs reduce the capital on which returns accrue in all subsequent years, the gap between the two lines grows ever faster.

bloecke.titel: Effect of a cost difference of 1.3 percentage points (illustrative calculation, before tax)
kopf: Share of the low-cost final value

bloecke.md: The difference of 1.3 percentage points a year reduces final wealth after thirty years by almost a third. This is where most discussions about costs go wrong. A fee is perceived as a share of the return (“1.5% of 7% is a fifth”), but it is deducted from capital. Capital that has flowed out as a fee earns no returns in any of the following years.

## Bogle, Vanguard and the index fund for private investors

The idea is older than the product. As early as his senior thesis at Princeton (1951), John C. Bogle argued that mutual funds could make no claim to outperform the market average. Almost a quarter of a century later, in 1974, he founded the fund company Vanguard. Its ownership structure sets it apart from other providers. The company is owned by its own US funds and thus by their investors; there are no external owners. As a result, no profit has to flow to third parties, and economies of scale benefit investors in the form of falling fees.

The first S&P 500 index fund for private investors followed in 1976. The offering was regarded as a failure, because it raised $11 million instead of the targeted sum. The industry mocked the product as “Bogle's Folly”, that is, a fund for people who settle for mediocrity. In November 1999, the same fund managed around $100 billion.

bloecke.unter: More than fifty years passed between the first formulation of the idea and its widespread adoption. Cost arguments gain ground slowly because nobody earns money from them.

ereignisse.text: Bogle concludes that funds can claim no superiority over the market averages.
The company is owned by its own funds. Its fees therefore only cover costs and are not a source of profit.
The fund starts with $11 million instead of the planned sum and is mocked in the industry as “Bogle's Folly”.
The essay “The Arithmetic of Active Management” provides an argument that needs no empirical data.
The fund, derided at first, reaches assets of $100 billion in November.
At the end of June 2026, the assets under management of the European ETF market rise to €3,099.5 billion for the first time.

bloecke.md:
## How widespread index funds are today

According to estimates, around $22 trillion is invested in index funds worldwide (as of May 2026). The figure depends heavily on the definition used and comes from secondary sources, so it is only useful as an order of magnitude. The European data are better documented. At the end of June 2026, ETF assets in Europe stood at €3,099.5 billion, of which only around €108 billion, or just under 3.5%, was in actively managed ETFs. The European ETF market therefore remains almost entirely a market for index funds.

In Germany, the idea has spread in the form of savings plans. In Germany and continental Europe, there were around 15.1 million savings plan executions a month in 2025. How much further this development will go cannot be seriously predicted. Earlier industry estimates for 2026 were clearly missed.

## Taxes as an additional cost factor

For investors in Germany, a second, often underestimated factor comes on top of the fee: the tax on realised gains. Capital income is subject to [[Flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)|flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)]] of 25% plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge under Sections 32d and 43a EStG (Income Tax Act), so effectively 26.375%, plus church tax where applicable. Funds that commit in their investment conditions to investing more than 50% continuously in equity participations count as equity funds under Section 2(6) InvStG (Investment Tax Act). For units in such funds, Section 20 InvStG grants a [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]] of 30%. The [[Saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag)|saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag)]] is €1,000 per person per year (Section 20(9) EStG).

As long as the units remain in the portfolio, the distributions are taxed in the case of a distributing fund; in the case of an accumulating fund, only the [[Advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)|advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)]] under Section 18 InvStG is due. It is calculated as the redemption price at the start of the year × base interest rate (Basiszins) × 0.7, reduced by distributions and capped at the increase in value achieved. The base interest rate for 2026 is 3.20% (BMF circular of 13 January 2026), so the base return is 2.24% of the value at the start of the year. An investor who switches funds because another one has done better recently, by contrast, realises the full gain in one go. This eliminates the deferral effect, that is, the compound interest on the tax amount that stays in the portfolio until the sale.

A portfolio is worth €50,000, of which €20,000 is unrealised price gain in an equity fund. The saver's allowance has already been used up by other income.

- Taxable after the 30% partial exemption: €20,000 × 70% = €14,000
- Tax: €14,000 × 26.375% = €3,692.50

Around €3,700 therefore flows out of the portfolio. That is about 7.4% of the portfolio value, even before the rest is invested in the new fund. At a 6% return p.a., this amount would have grown to just under €12,000 in twenty years (illustrative calculation, before tax). The new fund first has to make up this shortfall. According to research on persistence, there is no reliable indication that it will succeed.

The arithmetic does not say that no fund can beat the market, because many funds manage to do so every year. Nor does it say that index funds are safe. A world ETF loses just as much in a crash as the market it tracks.

In addition, it refers to something different from the well-known fund statistics. Sharpe's statement concerns the capital-weighted average of all active euros in a market. SPIVA and similar analyses, by contrast, count funds with equal weights and cover only some of the active investors. The results of the two approaches can therefore diverge. A year in which the majority of funds in a category do better than the market does not refute the identity.

A legitimate objection concerns price discovery. The arithmetic says nothing about whether prices are correct. It only describes the distribution of returns around the market. Price discovery is carried out by active market participants, and on average they bear the costs of it themselves. According to estimates by Vanguard, ICI, BlackRock and S&P Dow Jones, index strategies account for only around 1% to 10% of trading volume because of their low turnover. Prices are set by high-frequency traders, hedge funds and private investors. Holdings and share of trading are therefore two different metrics. The detailed debate on concentration, index effects and Michael Burry's thesis follows in the lesson on whether passive investing is a bubble.

If you accept the arithmetic, the starting question in fund selection changes. Instead of searching for the best fund, you clarify three points: which market you want to own, what you pay for it each year and how long you leave the investment unchanged. The first two can be decided and checked in advance; the third depends on your own behaviour. None of the three requires a talent for forecasting.

mitnehmen: Before costs, the average actively managed euro earns exactly the market return. This statement is an identity and not a statistic, so no study can refute it.
After costs, the market average is therefore above the capital-weighted average of active investors.
Costs reduce capital and therefore all later returns. A difference of 1.3 percentage points a year costs around 31% of final wealth over thirty years.
Bogle's idea holds regardless of whether markets are efficient. It only assumes that gross return minus costs equals net return.
In Germany, every fund switch is also a taxable event. Tax of 26.375% on 70% of the gain leaves the portfolio, and this amount earns no further returns afterwards.

begriffe.text: Fund that replicates an index instead of making its own selection decisions. Its goal is the index return minus its own costs. Most ETFs are exchange-traded index funds, but there are also actively managed ETFs.

Principle formulated by John Bogle according to which gross return minus costs equals net return, regardless of the efficiency of markets. Costs are the only factor influencing return that an investor knows in advance and determines themselves.

begriffe.begriff: Arithmetic of active management (Arithmetik der aktiven Verwaltung)
begriffe.text: Identity described by William Sharpe (1991). Since all investors together hold the market, the capital-weighted average of actively managed money earns exactly the market return before costs and necessarily less after costs.
Weighting of the securities in a portfolio by their market capitalisation. Only with this weighting does a portfolio reproduce the market to scale. Sharpe's argument is based on this.
